notes:
Most of what I found comes from older verse-by-verse commentaries on biblehub, studylight and blueletterbible, plus Enduring Word. I didn't find anything from Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, NET Bible study-note, Bible Odyssey or prosperity/word-of-faith sources. I also found no real split between Protestant traditions on this chapter. The one real debate is over how to translate v. 4, and it's a question of language, not denomination.

Two notes on sources: I read the Pulpit Commentary and Calvin pages in full, but my tool didn't give me citable sentence markers for them. Points from those two pages are therefore given with their URLs but without citation tags.

**v. 1**
- **Background:** Hezekiah's reign, about 705–701 BC. Judah's leaders were thinking about a defence pact with Egypt against Sennacherib of Assyria. Historical Background • Timeframe: About 705–701 BC, during King Hezekiah's reign. Assyria, led by Sennacherib, was rolling over the ancient Near East. Judah's leaders weighed a defensive pact with Egypt, hoping chariots could counter Assyrian infantry. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/31.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Judah committed two sins: trusting Egypt's army, and not looking to the Holy One of Israel. They found reasons to trust chariots and horsemen but none to trust God. Isaiah confronted Judah with two sins: the sin of trusting in Egypt and their military might, and the sin of not looking to the Holy One of Israel. He quotes Trapp's picture of standing with "one foot on a rock, and another foot upon a quicksand". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-31/
- **Ellicott:** Judah's leaders wanted Egyptian cavalry to shore up their weakest point. Isaiah calls this trusting an "arm of flesh." The princes of Judah were attracted by the prospect of strengthening themselves in their weakest point, and reinforcing the cavalry of Judah... Isaiah once more condemns this as trusting in an "arm of flesh" instead of in the "Holy One of Israel." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/31-1.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** Their sin was more than trusting a creature. They also failed to look to God in faith or to seek him in prayer. Their sin lay not only in their confidence in the creature, but in their neglect of the Lord himself. Same URL.
- **Geneva Study Bible:** Two reasons not to ally with Egypt. God had forbidden a return there (Deut 17:16) so they wouldn't forget their redemption, and Egypt's idolatry could corrupt them. You can't trust both God and worldly things. first, because the Lord had commanded them never to return there... and secondly, lest they should be corrupted with the superstition and idolatry of the Egyptians... for they cannot trust in both. Same URL.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Samaria, Gaza and Ashdod had already shown that Egypt couldn't be relied on, yet Judah still trusted it. Egypt was the only power that seemed able to match Assyria's chariots. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God doesn't condemn ordinary, lawful means of safety, as long as people don't deny God's power. The sin is clinging to outward means without seeking God, or using forbidden means because you distrust his promises. Calvin applies the verse widely: anything that pulls our minds away from God becomes our "Egypt." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/31.htm
- **Translation note:** The NET Bible renders the opening "woe" as "Those who go down to Egypt for help are as good as dead". https://biblehub.com/lexicon/isaiah/31-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **Pulpit:** Calling God "wise" is intense irony. Judah's human advisers aren't the only wise ones; God could give good counsel if anyone asked. The "evildoers" are the Jews and their "help" is the Egyptians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The "house of miscreants" means Judah itself (compare Isa 1:4). He will not set aside His threatening words, but carry them out. The house of miscreants is Judah (Isaiah 1:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/31-1.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** You think you are safe, in engaging the Egyptians; but God is not inferior to them in wisdom or strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/31.htm
- **Ironside:** Whether He speaks in grace or in judgment, He will never go back on His word... His faithfulness abides whether we believe it or not. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-31.html
- **Calvin:** Isaiah is mocking the leaders' scheming. Secret plans only provoke God more, because he "taketh the wise in their own craftiness." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/31.htm

**v. 3**
- **Pulpit:** In Egypt, Pharaoh was treated as a kind of god, and Judah relied on him that way. Isaiah insists the Egyptians are mere men, and their horses are just animals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm
- **Geneva:** "He that helpeth" and "he that is helped" are both the Egyptians and the Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/isaiah-31.html
- **Wesley:** "Flesh" means weak and frail. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-31.html
- **A Protestant–Catholic point:** Calvin draws a doctrinal lesson here. When man is set against God, nothing worthy of praise is left to man. He says this is why Protestants can't agree with "the Papists" on free will, merit and the cause of salvation: all of salvation must be credited to God alone. Calvin is describing his opponents here; I found no Catholic source giving its own reading of the verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/31.htm

**v. 4: the main debate**
- **Traditional reading, God protects Zion.** Guzik says God would protect Mount Zion if Judah trusted Him or not. (enduringword URL above). Matthew Henry says God will destroy the Assyrian army as easily and irresistibly... as a lion tears a lamb in pieces. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/31-4.html
- **Wesley:** He stresses grace given though not deserved: yet the Lord himself will, of his own grace, give you that help which you do not deserve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/31.htm
- **Calvin:** God attaches a promise to his ban on seeking help elsewhere, so no one can say he leaves them hopeless. "The Lord assists, and will assist; he forbids you to ask assistance from the Egyptians." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/31.htm
- **The translation question:** The preposition has been differently rendered as for, on, against. Ellicott explains the "against" view: God would use the Assyrians to punish Jerusalem and let no outsider interfere. He still concludes that, given v. 5, the idea of protection seems more natural than that of hostility. Keil & Delitzsch translate it descend to the campaign against the mountain of Zion. Another note on the same page points out that elsewhere the phrase means "fight against" (Isa 29:7–8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/31-4.htm
- **Pulpit:** Grammatically, "fight against" is possible, but the words can instead go with "come down," giving "on Mount Zion." The best commentators are of opinion that this must be the sense. The words are a promise, not a threat. Same URL.
- **Trapp:** Verses 4 and 5 show God's power and God's mercy, the two main pillars and supports of trust in God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/isa-31.cfm

**v. 5**
- **The bird image:** Pulpit calls it birds hovering, or fluttering, over their young, to protect them. A second simile, expressive of tenderness, as the former one was of power and strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm
- **"Pass over":** Barnes notes that the Hebrew word is the one used for the Passover (Exod 12) and means to spare or preserve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/31-5.htm
- **Wesley:** The destroying angel shall pass over Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/31.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** God had been moving against Jerusalem through Assyria. Here his attitude changes suddenly, into that of birds circling their threatened nests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/31-5.htm
- **Applied to Christ:** Barnes thinks Jesus may have had this verse in mind in Matthew 23:37, the hen gathering her chicks. Maclaren (Baptist) applies the Passover picture to faith in Christ: Only by our individual faith in Jesus Christ as our individual Saviour can we put the blood on our door-posts. Both on the same URL.

**v. 6**
- **Pulpit:** Isaiah speaks of Israel in the third person out of tenderness, not to hurt their feelings by mingling with promise an open rebuke. That quote is from the full Pulpit page, as it appears on studylight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-31.html
- **Calvin:** He translates the verse a little differently: "Return according as you have made a deep revolt." However deep their sin, it doesn't shut the door on repentance. But true repentance needs real grief over sin, not a half-repentance, together with hope of pardon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/31.htm
- **Geneva:** Isaiah touches their conscience that they might earnestly feel their grievous sins, and so truly repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/isaiah-31.html

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** Repentance means turning towards God, and away from anything we have put in God's place. (enduringword URL above)
- **Pulpit:** On the day Assyria is defeated, people will see idols for what they are. They didn't help Assyria, so how could they help Judah? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm
- **Calvin:** Verse 6 calls for repentance; verse 7 shows its fruit. Repentance lives in the heart, so it has to show itself in deeds, as a tree is known by its fruit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/31.htm

**v. 8**
- **Fulfilment:** Most sources link this to 2 Kings 19:35 / Isaiah 37:36. Guzik writes that God simply sent the angel of the LORD and killed 185,000 Assyrians in one night. Wesley: Not of any man, but of an angel. (enduringword and wes URLs above)
- **Barnes:** "Sword" is a figure of speech for total destruction, not a literal sword. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-31.html
- **"Forced labour":** Pulpit reads it "shall be for tribute," meaning they will become another power's vassals. Wesley says the Hebrew means "shall melt away," with hearts melting in fear. (Pulpit and studylight Wesley URLs above)

**v. 9**
- **"Their rock":** Pulpit says recent commentators (Kay, Delitzsch, Cheyne) generally take this as Assyria's king, set against his princes. It links this to Sennacherib's hurried flight to Nineveh (Isa 37:37). Wesley takes the older reading, that Sennacherib flees to his strong city of Nineveh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/31.htm
- **Fire and furnace:** In Pulpit's words, God was both a light to his people and "a consuming Fire" (Hebrews 12:29) to his enemies. His presence, indicated by the Shechinah in the holy of holies, was at once for blessing and for burning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/31.htm Wesley reads it the same way: fire to defend his people, and to consume their enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-31.html
